challenges.claim: observed_substrate_signals says a 'second-person address to the primeval waters runs 104:6-9', but the second-person forms in that stretch address Yahweh, while the waters are the third-person-plural subjects.
challenges.evidence: Spliced from verse_map_oshb.json (all byte tier at their own refs): web:Ps.104.6 = oshb:Ps.104.6 has כִּסִּית֑וֹ; web:Ps.104.7 = oshb:Ps.104.7 has the 2ms-suffixed noun גַּעֲרָ֣תְךָ֣ and the 3mp verbs יְנוּס֑וּן and יֵחָפֵזֽוּן; web:Ps.104.9 = oshb:Ps.104.9 has שַׂ֭מְתָּ with the 3mp verbs יַֽעֲבֹר֑וּן and יְ֝שׁוּב֗וּן. A rebuke and a thunder-voice suffixed to the addressee cannot belong to the fleeing party, and WEB reads the same split: “At your rebuke they fled. At the voice of your thunder they hurried away.” (web:Ps.104.7) and “You covered it with the deep as with a cloak” (web:Ps.104.6). The addressee across 104:6-9 is Yahweh; the waters are the third-person subject. Since a scene/addressee shift is a tier-1 driver in this book, an addressee named wrongly is a substrate error in a dependent field, not a wording preference.

challenges.evidence: Spliced from verse_map_oshb.json: web:Ps.104.24 = oshb:Ps.104.24 has כֻּ֭לָּם (U+05DB U+05BC U+05BB U+05AD U+05DC U+05BC U+05B8 U+05DD); web:Ps.104.27 = oshb:Ps.104.27 has כֻּ֭לָּם (U+05DB U+05BC U+05BB U+05AD U+05DC U+05BC U+05B8 U+05DD) -- byte-equal codepoint sequences. sweep.py --heb on that pointed form returns 2 verses book-wide, counted as verses, and they are exactly these two (MT Ps.104.24 and Ps.104.27); the accented token occurs nowhere else in the book, so this is a pointed-byte fact and not a skeleton artefact -- the bare consonantal string returns 15 verses because it also matches the 3mp-suffixed noun standing at MT Ps.104.21 and again inside Ps.104.27 itself. At 104:24 its antecedent is the works of Yahweh, which WEB renders “In wisdom, you have made them all” (web:Ps.104.24), i.e. creation broadly -- the very referential class the row assigns exclusively to 104:27 with “These all wait for you” (web:Ps.104.27). A repeated byte-true token spanning the cut is cross-seam cohesion evidence and must be disclosed and answered; as written it is instead cited as the driver for the cut it straddles.

challenges.claim: The shift at 104:27 is recorded as an addressee-class shift, but the addressee is Yahweh continuously from 104:24 through 104:30; what changes is the third-person referent, which is a weaker signal class than the tier-1 addressee shift the label invokes.
challenges.evidence: The sea creatures of 104:25-26 are never addressed: 104:26 speaks of them in the third person while addressing Yahweh with the 2ms perfect at web:Ps.104.26 = oshb:Ps.104.26 יָצַ֥רְתָּ, and 104:24 addresses Yahweh vocatively -- “Yahweh, how many are your works!” (web:Ps.104.24). Across 104:27-30 the addressee is the same: “These all wait for you” (web:Ps.104.27), “You open your hand” (web:Ps.104.28). Since scene and addressee shifts are a named tier-1 driver class in this book, labelling a third-person referent change as an addressee-class shift overstates the tier of the evidence actually present.

The accents differ at both words -- U+05A5 and U+0597 at 104:1 against U+05A3 and U+05AD at 104:35 -- so raw byte-equality is false, and collate.py of the 104:1 run against the MT Ps.104.35 window returns tier accent_stripped. The row's own rationale prints the correct closing bytes at web:Ps.104.35 = oshb:Ps.104.35 בָּרֲכִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי, so the signal field contradicts the rationale field of the same row while naming the one tier the campaign treats as quotation-grade. The inclusio itself survives at accent_stripped and skeleton tier and needs only the tier named correctly.

challenges.claim: device_notes states that hallelu-Yah opens and closes the two following psalms, but the first of them does not open with hallelu-Yah at all -- it opens with the hodu formula.
challenges.evidence: psalm_device_inventory.json lists Ps.105 only under halleluyah verse_final (Ps.105.45) and lists Ps.105.1 under hodu_openings alongside MT Ps.33.2, Ps.107.1, Ps.118.1, Ps.118.29 and Ps.136.1. The bytes agree: web:Ps.105.1 = oshb:Ps.105.1 opens הוֹד֣וּ, not the frame form that stands at web:Ps.104.35 = oshb:Ps.104.35 הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ. Only the second of the two psalms carries the frame on both ends (halleluyah verse_initial Ps.106.1 and verse_final Ps.106.48). The sentence is offered as texture rather than evidence, but it is still a false factual statement in row prose about a tier-1 frame device, and it is contradicted by the curated inventory the same field elsewhere relies on.

challenges.claim: device_notes puts curly double quotes around a transliteration and an English gloss of a Hebrew verb, but the book-wide convention reserves curly double quotes for WEB text so that the quote checker can tell the two apart.
challenges.evidence: check_web_quotes.py over the 8-row extract returns flag_count 2; the second is on this row's device_notes: quote 'they will praise', refs_nearby empty, issue 'curly quote with NO web: ref in its field'. The flagged string is a gloss of the verb form at web:Ps.22.26 = oshb:Ps.22.27, not WEB text, and the adjacent transliteration is curly-quoted in the same way. Under the quote convention both belong in straight quotes; the underlying observation about the consonantal false positive is correct and needs no change.
